sections.body:
A hotel is a building that rents you a bed for a number of nights, and it is also a service system with rules that are mostly written down somewhere you have not read. The rules are not meant to trap you. They exist because a hotel sells the same room to many different people and has to protect the ones who are not there yet.

Check-in is the moment you take the room. It normally happens between 14:00 and 15:00, and **check-out** is the moment you give the room back, usually between 10:00 and 12:00. Both times are written on your booking. Most hotels will store your bag for free if you arrive early or leave late, which means you can usually arrive at any hour without paying for a night you did not sleep in.

The desk is where the room changes hands, and it is also where money, identity and rules meet. In the order it usually happens: the desk looks at your **ID and the name on the booking**, finds the reservation, takes a payment or a **deposit**, gives you the **room key** and the room number, and tells you two times: breakfast hours and check-out time.

Behind the desk works a small chain of staff: the **receptionist** who deals with you now, the **concierge** who arranges tickets and taxis, and **housekeeping**, the team that cleans the rooms. Each has a different job, and a good traveller knows which one to ask.

Everything else in this article is built on one idea: a hotel is a service, and services are given when you ask clearly. A request that is stated in one sentence, with a reason, is usually granted. A complaint that is vague is usually explained away.

A hotel also has a geography, and the floor plan tells you what you will hear. The **entrance and lobby** are where the noise is: doors, trolleys, conversations, a queue for check-out. The **corridor** is the worst place for a room if you need quiet, because it carries every door and every suitcase wheel. The **top floor** is usually the quietest, often the most expensive, and the furthest from the lift. Rooms over the **kitchen, the bar or the laundry** run warm and noisy.

None of this is hidden, and the price difference between rooms is largely this: distance from the noise. If sleeping well matters to you, ask for a specific floor and a specific position when you book, not when you arrive.
examples: I have a reservation under the name Nguyen, for three nights.
Can I leave my bags here until this afternoon?
sections.heading: What a hotel actually is, and what check-in means

sections.body:
Almost every problem at a hotel desk can be solved before you get to the desk, and the time to do it is while you are waiting for your flight.

Confirm the booking in writing. You should have a confirmation with the address, the check-in and check-out times, the number of nights, the room type and what it says about payment. If the confirmation says "pay at property", you are expected to pay at the desk, and the card may be charged at the full rate plus taxes. If it says the price is prepaid and non-refundable, the room is paid for and cannot be changed. Both are fine; being surprised by them is not.

Check the address, not just the name. Hotels with similar names sit a few streets apart, and some sit far from the airport or the station. Copy the address into your phone in the local script as well, because you may have to show it to a driver who does not read Latin letters.

Know what is included. Breakfast may be included, may cost extra, or may be a voucher for a fixed meal. Some hotels in Europe do not serve breakfast at all, and the nearest bakery is often better. The swimming pool may be closed for repairs, and the Wi-Fi may be limited to a certain number of devices. Check the "what is included" list rather than the photographs.

Send your arrival time and flight number. If you land late, tell the hotel. Many hotels stop holding a room after a cut-off hour, and after that the room may be given away and your reservation cancelled. A note on the booking saying "arriving 23:40, flight TG 831" takes thirty seconds and often saves a night.

Check the cancellation terms once more. Free cancellation until 18:00 on the day of arrival is the normal, fair arrangement. If the terms are worse than that, you know to call before the deadline rather than after.
examples: I am arriving at 23:40 on flight TG 831. Can you note that on my booking?
Is breakfast included, and what are the hours?
What is the address in the local language?
sections.heading: Before you arrive, so the desk is easy

sections.body:
These are the words you will hear at the desk, in almost any language, and what each one means in practice.

Reservation is your booking: a room held for you, with a name, a date and a rate. **Confirmation** is the document proving it. **Walk-in** is someone who arrives with no booking; walk-in rates are often higher, but a hotel will sometimes offer a walk-in a better room if the booked type is full.

Deposit is a sum of money the hotel holds on your card, or takes in cash, against extras and damage. It is not a payment for the room if you have already paid. It is released after you leave, but the bank can take several working days to put it back.

Room key is the card or fob that opens the door. In many modern hotels the key is also the room number, the lift access and the breakfast voucher. Losing it is charged, so keep it with you.

Check-out is giving the room back and paying the final bill. **Late check-out** is being allowed to stay a few hours longer; some hotels give it free, some charge a half-day rate, and the desk can usually confirm at check-in rather than at 11:00 on the last morning.

Luggage storage or **left luggage** is the service that holds your bags before you check in or after you check out. It is normally free for hotel guests, and it is the reason you can arrive eight hours early and still use the city.

Incidentals are the extras: minibar drinks, the safe, the city phone, laundry, a missing towel. They are charged to the card you gave at the desk, which is why you should give a card you are willing to see a temporary hold on.
examples: Is the deposit on my card released after check-out?
I need a second key card.
Could I have an invoice for the company?
sections.heading: The words the desk will use on you

terms.example: Check-in is from 14:00, but I can leave my bags with you in the morning.
terms.gloss: The moment you take the room, normally from 14:00 or 15:00. Before it, the hotel usually stores your luggage free of charge.

terms.example: Could I have a second key card for my colleague?
terms.gloss: The card or fob that opens your door. In many hotels it also works as your room number, your lift pass and your breakfast voucher.

terms.example: We hold a deposit of 200 on your card for the minibar and the safe.
terms.gloss: A sum held on your card, or taken in cash, to cover extras and damage. It is released after you leave.

terms.example: Can I check out at 14:00 instead of 11:00? My flight is at 17:00.
terms.gloss: Giving the room back and paying the final bill, usually between 10:00 and 12:00. Late check-out can often be arranged.

terms.example: Could you store my luggage until my flight in the evening?
terms.gloss: Free storage of bags before check-in or after check-out, which lets you use the city without carrying a suitcase.

sections.body:
Check-in is a short conversation with five parts. Doing them in this order means one trip to the desk instead of three.

Have the booking ready. Open the confirmation on your phone, with the name and the address, so you are not digging in an inbox while a queue grows behind you. If the name on your passport differs from the booking, say so now; it is much easier to fix before the room is assigned.

State your needs first, if you have them. A late arrival, a quiet room, a high floor, a twin bed instead of a double, or a connecting door. The desk can often solve these in one sentence, and it is easier to ask before you have the key.

Give the payment. The hotel needs a card for the deposit and the extras, and sometimes for the whole stay. Say what it is: "I would like to pay the room now and leave a deposit on the card", or "Can we settle the room at check-out?" You may be offered a foreign exchange rate if you pay in another currency; check the rate before you accept it, because the hotel's rate is usually worse than the card company's.

Take the key and the two times. The room number, breakfast hours and check-out time. Write the check-out time down somewhere you will see it, because it is the one fact that decides the shape of your last morning.

Then take the lift. Do not stand at the desk and read the paper while the queue grows. Move aside and read it at the desk edge or in the lobby.
examples: I am checking out late, my flight is at 19:30.
Can I settle the bill at check-out instead?
Could I have a quiet room on a high floor, if one is free?
sections.heading: Checking in, in the order that avoids a queue
steps: Open the booking confirmation and check the name on it.
Say your arrival time, and any special request, first.
Show your passport or ID for the check-in.
Ask what is charged now and what is charged at the end.
Take the key, the room number, breakfast hours and check-out time.
Ask for an invoice if you need one for your employer.

sections.body:
You have one job in the first five minutes of a room: find the problems while the hotel can still fix them easily. After you unpack, every problem becomes an argument about who was told what and when.

Start with the **door and the lock**. Does the key open it on the first try? Some rooms need the key card held still, others need a tap. If the door does not latch, tell the desk, because a room that does not lock is a security problem, not a comfort problem.

Then the **bathroom**: is there hot water, is the water clean, does the shower drain, is there a towel, is there hot water for the sink as well as the shower. A hotel with no hot water is a problem you want to know about before you are tired.

Then the **bed**: is it clean, is the linen changed, are there stains, is the mattress comfortable enough for two nights. Say it plainly and early: "There are stains on the duvet. Could the room be changed?" You are far more likely to get another room than a clean-up if you ask in the first hour.

Then the **equipment**: does the air conditioning work, do the sockets work, is the safe large enough for your passport and your laptop, does the television work, is there a hair dryer. Record any fault with a photograph on your phone. A photo of the wall stain you complained about protects you from being charged for it later.

Then the **noise**: stand in the corridor for ten seconds and listen. A room over the lift, next to the ice machine or behind the bar has a permanent noise pattern. If it is bad, ask to move, and move early, because hotels can usually reassign a room the same evening.

Finally, **the wi-fi**: get the password and test it on your phone before you need it. Networks in hotels often require a room number or a surname, and the password on the desk card is sometimes for the previous guest.
examples: There is no hot water in this room. Could you send someone?
The air conditioning is not working. Is another room possible?
Could you take a photo of the stain on the desk for me?
sections.heading: The five-minute room check, before you unpack

sections.body:
Hotels use a small set of pictograms, and they are worth learning because they tell you what the hotel offers before you ask.

The **Wi-Fi** symbol with radiating lines means there is a network, and the speed or the number of devices is often written next to it. **Breakfast** is a cup, a fork and knife, and a clock beside them gives the hours. A **pool** symbol means the pool exists, not that it is open: a covered or crossed-out symbol means closed.

A **luggage** symbol marks the bell desk, the place where bags are stored and where taxis are arranged. A **key** symbol on a board in the lobby is the message board where staff post the name of a guest who is expecting a visitor, or the phone number of a taxi driver waiting outside.

Do not disturb and **clean my room** are door cards in every language of the world. A round card on the door handle means one thing, a rectangular one another. If you put out the cleaning card before 14:00 you will usually get the room cleaned that day, and if you put it out later you get it next morning.

And the green **emergency exit** signs point to the stairs. Look for them when you arrive. In a hotel, the two nearest stairs matter, because you should know how to reach them from your floor and where they lead.

Two more marks are worth recognising. A **luggage trolley** by the entrance means the hotel has trolleys, which sounds trivial and is not, at eleven at night with three bags. And a small board by the lifts listing room ranges and services is a summary of what the hotel actually does; read it once on arrival and it saves a trip to reception.
examples: The Wi-Fi is free, but there is a limit of two devices.
Breakfast is served from 6:30 to 10:00.
What time does the breakfast room close?
sections.heading: The signs around the hotel, and what they promise

symbols.meaning: Radiating lines: a wireless network is available. The speed or device limit is written beside it.
Cup and cutlery: breakfast. A clock next to it gives the hours it is served.
A suitcase: the bell desk, where bags are stored and taxis are called.
A key on a board: the guest message board.
A green running figure: the emergency exit and the stairs.

sections.body:
A good hotel has more to offer than the room, and most travellers never find out what it is. The people who can unlock most of it are the **concierge** and the desk staff. Ask them the same way every time: name what you need, say when you need it, and say why if it helps.

Housekeeping cleans the room, usually once a day, and takes away the towels you leave on the floor. If you need fresh towels, call the desk and say how many. If you want the room cleaned again today, say so early, because the team works floor by floor and the last rooms of the day are the hardest to reach.

Laundry works in two ways. Some hotels have a self-service laundry room with machines you pay for. Others run a wash-and-return service: you leave the clothes before a stated hour, and they come back folded, usually with a charge per item or per kilogram. Ask about the price and the timing before you commit, because same-day service normally means dropping the bag before 10:00.

The concierge sells the things a hotel cannot: tickets, tours, a table at a restaurant that is fully booked, a doctor, a visa appointment. In a popular city the concierge is the difference between a sold-out day and a good day. A polite, specific request gets better results than a vague one.

Small practical things: an extra towel, an extra pillow, a different pillow for a stiff neck, an iron, an adapter, a hairdryer, more hangers, a quiet alarm clock. These cost the hotel almost nothing and are usually delivered within the hour. Ask for them early, and they become the reason the room is remembered well.

Distance and time: ask the desk how long it takes to the station, to the airport, and to the old town at that hour of the day, and whether you should take the train or a taxi. They will know the answer for the hour you are asking about, and they will know the traps.
examples: Could you call a taxi to the airport for 5:00 in the morning?
Is there a laundry service, and what is the same-day cut-off?
Do you have an adapter for a European socket?
sections.heading: During the stay: asking for what a hotel can do

terms.example: Could housekeeping bring two more towels, please?
terms.gloss: The team that cleans the rooms, changes the linen and takes away used towels.

terms.example: The concierge booked a table at a restaurant that was fully booked.
terms.gloss: The staff member who arranges tickets, tours, taxis, doctors and anything else the hotel does not sell itself.

sections.body:
Not reading the deposit terms. A hotel may hold several hundred on your card, and some hotels take cash only against a card. Ask the amount before you hand over the card, not after.

Accepting a currency conversion at the desk. "Would you like to pay in dollars or euros?" sounds helpful and is usually a bad rate. Choose to be charged in the local currency and let your own bank do the conversion.

Leaving the minibar key. Some hotels now place a sensor in the fridge, and a bottle taken and replaced still gets billed. If you take anything from the minibar, tell the desk, and pay for it before you leave.

Leaving things in the safe after you check out. The hotel will charge for opening it, and the charge lands on your card weeks later, in a currency you did not expect.

Missing the check-out time and being charged a full extra night. Most hotels are strict about this, and some charge the full night rate rather than a day rate. Set an alarm.

Not asking for the receipt. Get the final invoice in writing, with the charges itemised, on the day you leave. Disputing a charge you cannot document is almost impossible.
sections.heading: Where travellers lose money in a hotel

sections.body:
Something will go wrong: the room is noisy, the air conditioning fails, the bill is wrong, or the room you booked is not the room you got. The way you handle it decides whether the hotel fixes it or argues with you.

Report it the same day, in writing. A message to the desk, or an email to the address on your confirmation, creates a record. Say what happened, when it happened, and what you would like. "The air conditioning in room 412 did not work between 22:00 and 02:00. I would like the room changed for tomorrow night" is a request a manager can act on. A complaint delivered at check-out, in words, with no room number, is not.

Ask for the person who can fix it. At the desk, ask for the manager or the duty manager. It is not a threat; it is the normal escalation in hotels, and most staff will be relieved to hand it over.

Do not shout in a lobby. Loudness is read as a bad mood, and a bad mood gets a bad outcome. Calm, specific and factual wins nearly every time.

Know what you can reasonably expect. If the room is genuinely not what was booked, the hotel should offer another room or a partial refund. If the problem is a minor inconvenience, a goodwill gesture is normal. If you were overcharged, ask for the charge to be removed with the invoice as proof.

And if it is not fixed, escalate outside the hotel. Many countries have a public tourism or consumer office that handles hotel complaints, and most hotels will act faster once you mention it. Keep the confirmation, the invoice, your photos and your messages. If you paid by card, a chargeback is a last resort, not a first move.

One thing to keep: most problems in a hotel are small and solvable, and the staff are usually on your side. The traveller who is calm, prepared and specific almost always gets what they need.
examples: Room 412 has no hot water. I have reported it twice; could you send someone now?
I would like the minibar charge of 18 removed, because I did not take anything.
Could I speak to the duty manager, please?
sections.heading: When something is wrong with the hotel

item.summary: A hotel desk is a negotiation with rules you cannot see. After reading this you can read a booking, check in without queues, check the room in five minutes, ask for what you need, and leave without a surprise on the bill.
item.title: Checking Into a Hotel Like a Pro
